BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: A pair of weak upper level troughs will move through on Thursday and Friday, bringing a 10-30% chance of showers to northern areas. QPF totals are expected to stay under 0.10" for both events combined.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Breezy early this week. Near to slightly above normal temperatures through the week.
- Dry today, then a slight chance of showers late Tuesday through Friday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Quiet conditions will persist through the short term period with no significant weather expected across southeast Oregon and southwest Idaho. Upper level ridging centered over the Pacific Northwest will provide dry weather and mostly clear skies tonight into Tuesday morning. Patchy valley fog or low stratus remains possible during the late night and early morning hours, mainly within sheltered mountain basins and river valleys.

A compact upper level low tracks eastward across the Great Basin on Tuesday. The primary impact from this system will be an increase in mid and high level cloud cover. There looks to be enough moisture and weak instability for a slight chance (15 to 20 percent) of light rain showers along the Idaho/Nevada border Tuesday afternoon and evening. Elsewhere, dry conditions will prevail with light winds.

The low will exit into the central Rockies on Wednesday while weak upper ridging rebuilds from the west. This will result in clearing skies and continued dry weather through Wednesday night. Temperatures will remain near to slightly above seasonal normals through the period, with daytime highs generally in the mid 50s to lower 60s in the valleys and upper 40s to lower 50s across the higher terrain. Lows will dip into the upper 20s and 30s for most locations.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: A pair of weak upper level troughs will move through on Thursday and Friday, bringing a 10-30% chance of showers to northern areas. QPF totals are expected to stay under 0.10" for both events combined. Snow levels will range from 5500-7000 ft MSL, so some of the higher peaks will see a light dusting. Temperatures will be near normal with light winds. An upper level ridge will build in over the weekend, with temperatures warming to 5-10 degrees above normal by Sunday. Another upper level trough will approach the Pacific Northwest early next week, ushering in low chances of showers by Monday night. Temperatures will be similarly warmer than normal on Monday with breezier conditions Sunday and Monday as the system approaches.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: From Thursday onward, ridging builds into our area once again. A trough could move through the upper-level flow to our north on Friday. For now, we expect any meaningful precipitation chances to remain north of our area as moisture continues to be lacking.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Light snow showers in the mountains tonight, with additional snow accumulations of 2 inches or less. Slick travel in spots through early Tuesday morning.
- Scattered rain showers tonight for the plains. A few snowflakes to a dusting possible for the Palmer Divide and northern Weld County. Very windy for the plains through early Tuesday morning.
- Another chance for some rain and snow for the mountains on Wednesday bringing light precipitation amounts.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Current radar shows rain showers ongoing for most of the plains with the heaviest rain over western Morgan County and eastern Adams County. Some light snow is occurring for the mountains, mainly north of I-70. With deep northerly flow still in place, rain/snow showers will remain possible through early Tuesday morning. For the high country, we expect very little additional accumulation of snow (perhaps an inch or two at most), so the Winter Weather Advisory was cancelled earlier this evening. Some light rain showers will remain possible for the Palmer Divide, eastern plains, and into most of the Denver metro. High-resolution guidance (including one of the last NAMnest and NAM runs) shows an additional 0.1"-0.2" of rain possible for western Washington county and adjacent areas with some isolated slightly higher amounts possible through the overnight. The chance remains for some snowflakes to mix in for the Palmer Divide to as far north as Akron as well as far northern Weld County given the decreasing snow levels. A dusting is possible for the Palmer Divide due to a trend of slightly lower snow levels tonight. The chance for precipitation should end between 6am and 9am Tuesday.

Gusty winds remain likely on the plains for the next few hours with some gusts of 50-55 mph still possible. Given the gusty winds, there is a near zero chance for fog this morning in northern Colorado unlike the last several days. Wind gusts of 30-35 mph will remain possible on Tuesday afternoon for the eastern plains. Otherwise, Tuesday will be a temperate day and feature warmer temperatures and more sun than Monday with upper-level ridging in control for our area. Highs should reach the mid 50s for the plains.

Wednesday brings the next storm system to our area, but it will move through quickly. A trough is forecast to move across Colorado from Wednesday afternoon through early Thursday. This system will lack in moisture, so any precipitation looks light in nature. Areas of the high country along the I-70 corridor and south look to be most favored for any light snow accumulations. Ensemble guidance is in good agreement that these locations should receive 1-3 inches of snow with perhaps some localized higher amounts at the highest elevations. DESI probabilities currently show that the chances for the heaviest snow in our area will be in the Mosquito Range. Some light rain showers will be possible for the Palmer Divide and our southeastern counties with an upslope component as the trough passes. The rest of the plains should stay dry. Any precipitation looks to quickly end on Wednesday night.

From Thursday onward, ridging builds into our area once again. A trough could move through the upper-level flow to our north on Friday. For now, we expect any meaningful precipitation chances to remain north of our area as moisture continues to be lacking. Guidance is in better agreement that another trough should move in from Canada down into the Great Plains just to our northeast towards the end of the weekend. This could introduce some gusty winds on Sunday for the eastern plains if momentum transfer is maximized as winds aloft could be rather strong. Otherwise, Thursday through Monday looks dry for our area. Temperatures should remain near average- in the upper 50s for the plains- through at least Saturday. The ridge look to strength and build into our area for Sunday and Monday, so temperatures could even reach the low to mid 60s for the plains on these days.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Monday...The slow warming trend continues as the flow aloft backs to westerly and with little if any cloud cover and 700 mb temperatures near 5 Celsius suggesting maximum temperatures from the upper 50s to mid 60s.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Rain and high elevation snow showers continue through Tuesday morning.
- Winter Weather Advisories remain in place for the mountains, higher elevations of the I-80 corridor and higher elevations of Niobrara County, with wet accumulating snow expected.
- Snow accumulation is possible along the Pine Ridge and the north side of the Cheyenne Ridge, but confidence is lower.
- Widespread northwest winds gusting 45 to 55 mph are expected along and east of the Laramie Range Monday and Monday night.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Snow began earlier this morning for areas west of the Laramie Range. Webcams and surface observations confirmed the snow, which was accumulating on grassy surfaces under pretty decent snowfall rates. Precipitation rates in these areas have begun to lessen as the surface low tracks further to the northeast, allowing some of the snow to melt thanks to the warmer ground temperature. The surface low tracking to the northeast is also producing some impressive wind gusts for areas east of the Laramie Range. Frequent gusts of 50 MPH are being observed. These strong gusts will continue into the evening hours, with the potential for an occasional 60 MPH wind gust through that timeframe. After midnight, winds will weaken, but still be quite blustery. Precipitation is beginning to fill in a bit more east of the Laramie Range. Temperatures here are predominately in the 40s so rain is still being observed. As snow levels drop to about 5000 feet this evening, rain will transition to snow, with the potential for accumulation, mainly along the Pine Ridge from the Niobrara/Converse County line to the Sioux/Dawes County line. Went ahead and issued a Winter Weather Advisory for Niobrara County as Lusk and the hills south of town could see between 2 and 4 inches of snow this evening and into tonight. Will also have to keep an eye on Harrison as they also have the potential to pick up a few inches of snow. The other area of concern will be the northern edge of the Cheyenne Ridge. Newer model guidance keeps placing several inches of snow here, however uncertainty is still high with amounts as it will largely depend on the snow levels. For now, will keep an eye on this area to see if any short-fuse winter headlines are needed. Other Winter Weather Advisories remain on track, with snow tapering off around the Arlington area this evening when the Advisory expires. The mountain zones and the South Laramie Range are also on track, with snow expected to continue through this evening, with additional accumulations up to 4 inches depending on location and elevation.

The weather on Tuesday looks quieter as the surface low pushes out of the area. Some lingering precipitation and wind could still be possible in the Nebraska panhandle during the morning hours, but will taper off by the afternoon. Decreasing clouds are expected throughout the day with mostly sunny skies anticipated by the afternoon. The increased sunshine will lead to warmer temperatures with highs in the 40s and low 50s. However, temperatures could be cooler based on the amount of snow cover.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Wednesday...Our region will be in between weather disturbances with a trough aloft over central Colorado, producing some cloud cover over our counties, but no precipitation. Temperatures slightly warmer than Tuesday with 700 mb temperatures near 0 Celsius.

Thursday...High amplitude and well pronounced ridging aloft will prevail across our counties, keeping the weather dry. The warming trend will continue, and with 700 mb temperatures near 2 Celsius, yielding maximum temperatures mainly in the 50s.
Friday...A progressive and positively tilted shortwave trough aloft moves across eastern Montana and eastern Wyoming, though with little if any cloud cover and no precipitation for our forecast area.
Saturday...Brisk northwest flow aloft prevails, and with decent low level pressure gradients, look for a windy and blustery day. Maximum temperatures should be slightly cooler than Friday.
Sunday...Transitory ridging aloft moves across our counties, with significant height rises aloft. 700 mb temperatures near 6 Celsius will yield high temperatures from the lower 50s to lower 60s.

Monday...The slow warming trend continues as the flow aloft backs to westerly and with little if any cloud cover and 700 mb temperatures near 5 Celsius suggesting maximum temperatures from the upper 50s to mid 60s.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: Models continue to sell broad high pressure building across the region to close out the week. This should help streamflows and soils to dry out.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Rivers across southwest CO and southeast UT remain high due to runoff. Several flood warnings will be in effect through Tuesday morning.
- Tuesday will be dry with below normal temperatures.
- A system is expected on Wednesday into Thursday morning. It will bring valley rain and mountain snow to the area. Amounts are generally minor.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Isolated snow showers are possible in the mountains overnight with minor accumulations. Other than that most locations will be dry and that continues into tomorrow. Given so much moisture and limited sun today, patchy fog is certainly possible in the favorable spots tonight. Tomorrow will be partly cloudy with temperatures 5-10 degrees below normal. This break will be short lived, as another low pressure works across the region on Wednesday. While moisture remains unimpressive with this system, a few showers and thunderstorms are expected Wednesday afternoon and overnight. Given the saturated soil there is concern for any additional rainfall. As of now the precipitation amounts are minor in comparison to the last event. Although thunderstorms could produce the rates for localized issues. We will continue to monitor this situation. The mountains should pick up another couple inches of snow too before the precipitation comes to an end Thursday morning.

Models continue to sell broad high pressure building across the region to close out the week. This should help streamflows and soils to dry out. Temperatures will remain cooler than normal, but a slight warm up is expected this weekend ahead of a potential pattern shift early next week.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Weak upper wave sneaks through the central Rockies late Wed into Thu morning, bringing widespread but generally light showers to many locations, heaviest Wed night.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Strong north winds and showers/isolated t-storms on the plains into this evening, perhaps some snow showers along the Palmer Divide overnight.
- Generally dry and breezy on Tue, strongest winds early in the day on the plains.
- Weak trough will bring scattered showers Wed into Wed night, early weekend system continues to look rather weak with just isolated showers over the mountains Fri night.
- Flooding will continue into mid-week along many waterways in the San Luis Valley, especially along the Conejos River and also the Rio Grande from Alamosa upstream.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Surface/mid level low pressure was located over sern CO early this afternoon, with nice area of post frontal deformation wrapping southward around the low across the I-25 corridor and southeast plains. Have even seen a few lightning strikes with heavier embedded precip, especially along and south of the Arkansas River where north winds were providing a little upslope boost to vertical motion and precip development. Precip has been mostly rain, though some occasional snow has mixed in over Teller County above 8000 feet. Farther west, scattered rain/mtn snow showers were gradually diminishing over the mountains and interior valleys, and expect precip here to continue to taper off into the evening. On the plains/I-25, already seeing signs of downslope drying in latest radar loop, with precip beginning to diminish and weaken from Pueblo northward into El Paso County. Expect this trend to continue through the afternoon into the evening, with bulk of precip ending up south of the Arkansas River by sunset as low pulls away and nly downslope increases. Brisk north winds then continue overnight into Tue morning, with precip gradually fading away at most locations, though HRRR suggest a few showers may redevelop along the Palmer Divide and near the KS border after midnight, lingering into early Tue morning. Precip could mix with or change to snow around Monument/Black Forest overnight, though expect any snow accumulations to be light given temps in the mid 30s.

On Tuesday, skies become mostly sunny by afternoon as clouds/precip shift east of the area. Still breezy/windy on the plains especially in the morning, with north winds gusting over 30 mph in the morning, then gradually diminishing from west to east during the afternoon. Max temps will remain rather cool despite the sun, with readings near/slightly below seasonal averages.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Weak upper wave sneaks through the central Rockies late Wed into Thu morning, bringing widespread but generally light showers to many locations, heaviest Wed night. Precip amounts will be under a quarter inch, but with snow levels falling toward 7000 feet by Thu morning, higher terrain locations could see a quick inch or two of snow before precip ends. Generally dry/mild weather then returns from Thu afternoon into Fri, before another weak wave brings back a few mountains showers Fri night/Sat morning. Weekend now looks dry and warmer as swrn upper ridge builds and main trough axis shifts eastward into the Great Lakes.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Following this system, strong ridging looks to build in across much of the western U.S. keeping conditions moderated through early next week.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Cool, dry, and stable conditions build into the forecast area through Wednesday.
- A weak system traverses the Great Basin on Wednesday bringing light valley rain and high elevation snowfall to northern and central Utah.
- Starting Thursday, quiet weather looks to persist as a strong ridge of high pressure builds across the western U.S..

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Mid-level ridging continues to build across the Great Basin with the departure of the system that brought notable rainfall to the forecast area. As such, height rises continue to occur across much of the western U.S. ushering in a brief period of quiet weather through Wednesday morning. Cold northwest mid-level flow will continue pumping cold air into the forecast area, keeping overnight temperatures tonight roughly 5F colder than normal with daytime highs tomorrow running 5-10F below normal.

On Wednesday, a compact weak shortwave trough will traverse the Great Basin bringing another round of light rain to lower elevation locations and light snowfall to higher terrain locations across northern and central UT. Given the moisture starved nature of this system and how quickly it will traverse east with time, no significant rainfall/snowfall is expected with this system. However, it will draw down some colder air keeping temperatures roughly 5-10F cooler than normal through Thursday morning.

Following this system, strong ridging looks to build in across much of the western U.S. keeping conditions moderated through early next week. With persistent height rises throughout the period, a warming trend appears likely starting Saturday, with temperatures warming to potentially as high as 5-10F above average across much of northern and central UT.

2660.travel_advice: Dangerous avalanche conditions. Careful snowpack evaluation, cautious route-finding and conservative decision-making essential.

product.author: Krista Beyer
bottom_line: Snowfall increases significantly as you climb in elevation due to high freezing levels during this storm. At the uppermost elevations, you can trigger avalanches where recent storm snow sits above a weak layer near the surface of the snowpack.

The most dangerous slopes face north, northeast, and east where winds drift snow onto lee slopes, forming thicker and more connected slabs. As you move down in elevation, avalanches will become smaller and more isolated.
You can find safer travel options at lower elevations and in wind-sheltered areas.

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Ian Fowler
bottom_line: Most slopes lack enough snow to produce an avalanche. If you find a steep slope with firm, continuous snow close to ridges, go around it to avoid the hazard. You can find this hazard at high elevations.

2842.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
hazard_discussion: Avalanche Forecasting Operations Have Come to a Close for the 2026-26 Season
Have a safe spring in the mountains. Continue to remain vigilant and flexible while traveling in the mountains this spring.
OBSERVATIONS

Observations are still greatly appreciated. Spring-time observations are extremely helpful as forecast operations have come to a close. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation to let the rest of the public know what's going on out there. Even a simple weather observation can be very useful.
• View recent observations HERE
• Submit an observation HERE
• Recent photos and videos HERE
Snow and Avalanche Information
• Dry Slab avalanche problems such as storm slab and wind slab avalanches are most likely during and immediately following a storm.

• Wet Loose avalanches are expected during warmups and (even brief) clear, sunny weather events, and rain events. Watch for pinwheels and rollerballs as an indicator the snow is becoming damp. If you're sinking into soft, mushy snow, it's time to turn around or find a different aspect.

• Wet Slab avalanches become likely during rain events and with multiple nights above freezing. Wet slabs occur when melt water pools and lubricates crusts or older persistent weak layers. Wet slab avalanches are notoriously difficult to predict.
• Cornices are large and often become unstable during prolonged warmups. Give yourself plenty of space above and below them. They tend to begin shedding during warming and/or rain events.
• Dry Loose Snow avalanches are expected during and immediately after a storm, particularly on shaded, north-facing slopes.

• Glide avalanches typically fail in similar spots year after year after an abundance of meltwater has saturated the ground or lower snowpack. Glide avalanches can occur in steep terrain, on smooth grassy slopes or on large slabs of rock. Look for glide cracks opening up during spring.
WEATHER
• Click HERE to view our Weather Station Map page with updated webcams
• Click HERE to view our Weather Tools page
• Spring weather patterns are often erratic and snow conditions can change quickly during spring weather. Be attentive to these changes and remain flexible with your travel plans.
• Rain on snow events can create dangerous avalanche conditions in a short period of time.
• Spring time means a higher sun angle, with direct solar radiation on the snowpack. Even a brief dose of sunshine can quickly alter the snow surface.

• Overcast skies and snow showers can open up to full sunshine in a matter of minutes. Convective snow showers can be spotty and difficult to forecast. Temperatures can vary depending on elevation and unexpected cloud cover can significantly alter a weather forecast.
OTHER CONSIDERATIONS
• Travel
• As people push into steeper, more consequential terrain, remember to maintain safe travel protocols and not let your guard down just because it's sunny and warm.
• During melt-freeze cycles, pay attention to "slide-for-life" circumstances, particularly during morning travel.
• Be mindful of terrain selection and timing. Identify terrain traps and be prepared to avoid/manage them.
• Spring Mindset

• Springtime is when mountain travelers push for bigger objectives. We have greater confidence in the stability of the snowpack and the high sun angle makes us feel ready to charge. As we start stepping out into bigger terrain in the mountains, be mindful of consequences (ask yourself, "If this slides, what will happen?"). Choose your terrain appropriately and manage new/surface snow problems accordingly. Be aware that dynamic weather can have quick impacts on the snow surface. A common theme I've noticed over the last 15 years playing in steep, snowy mountains is that experienced, seasoned people often get caught in small avalanches in big terrain during the spring. We have a tendency to underestimate "manageable" new snow problems like wind slab and loose snow. Pay attention to changing weather and know that small shifts in spring weather can have dramatic impacts on the upper snowpack.

(Precipitation data are recorded from Secesh SNOTEL site at 6540')

2735.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Ian Fowler
bottom_line: Most slopes are safe to travel on as they have very little snow. On high-elevation north-, northeast-, and east-facing slopes, if you find firm, hollow snow, you could trigger an avalanche. If in doubt, just walk around these drifts of snow.
